# byoa: the full docs

> byoa lets your app run each user's own Claude Code or Codex, on their plan and with their tools, in any sandbox, from inside your own backend.

This file has the full text of byoa's docs, for LLMs: the docs pages (https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs), SPEC.md, the agent skill and the to-do example, from https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa (branch main). The index is https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms.txt.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs

# byoa docs

**byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users power the AI in your app with their own AI subscription.**

Each user signs in to their own Claude or ChatGPT plan one time. When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code or Codex in a sandbox, with the user's tools, and streams the result back. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox.

byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0). It runs inside your app's own backend. It is not a hosted service. Start with [Getting started](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/getting-started.md). To learn the parts first, read [Concepts](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/concepts.md). To see which plans work, read [Supported AI subscriptions](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions.md).

These pages are the Markdown files in [docs/](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/docs) of the repository. The site at https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs shows the same pages, and serves each page as Markdown for LLMs (add `.md` to its address) and all of them in [llms-full.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms-full.txt).

## Start

- [Getting started](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/getting-started.md): install byoa, make one `agents` object, serve its two routes, sign a user in and run a first job
- [Concepts](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/concepts.md): who brings what, what byoa is and is not, how a job runs, and why real tokens never go into the sandbox
- [Supported AI subscriptions](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions.md): which Claude and ChatGPT plans your users can bring, and what each one gives
- [FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md): whether a user's AI account can get banned, and what an AI job costs with byoa and with an API key

# Getting started

This page takes you from `npm install` to a first agent job. Your app's backend makes one `agents` object, serves two routes, signs a user in to their own plan, and runs a job. A new app needs fewer than 50 lines of its own code for this. The [to-do example](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo) uses byoa in 35.

## Install

Install byoa from npm. Its package is `@madeyexz/byoa`, because npm does not allow the name `byoa`:

```sh
npm install @madeyexz/byoa
bun add @madeyexz/byoa
```

Also install the sandbox SDK that your app uses: `e2b` for E2B, `@daytona/sdk` for Daytona. Instabox and the local sandbox need none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. To use the newest commit on `main` before it is released, install from GitHub: `npm install github:madeyexz/byoa`.

## Make one `agents` object

Make one `agents` object in your backend: once for each process, or once in each Convex action.

```ts
import { createAgents } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { e2b } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b'
import { postgresStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres'

const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp',                                    // one app's AI logins are only this app's
  sandbox: e2b({ apiKey }),
  store: postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }),
  encryptionKey,                                   // openssl rand -base64 32; grants and AI logins are encrypted with it
  proxyUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/mcp',  // serve agents.proxy here
  oauth: { redirectUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/callback' },
})
```

- **`app`**: lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 24. It names the app's sandboxes and login volumes.
- **`sandbox`**: the [sandbox provider](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers.md). To change the provider, change this one line.
- **`store`**: your own database, through a [store adapter](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores.md). For Postgres, run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` once.
- **`encryptionKey`**: 32 random bytes as base64. Keep it the same between restarts, and keep it secret.
- **`proxyUrl`**: a public HTTPS URL. The sandbox must reach it. In development, use a tunnel such as `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`.

The default E2B template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it. Build it one time with `buildE2BTemplate()`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`. See [Sandbox providers](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers.md#e2b).

## Serve two routes

byoa's handlers are fetch handlers (`Request` → `Response`). On Node, wrap your app's handler with `toNodeListener` from `@madeyexz/byoa/node`.

```ts
if (url.pathname.startsWith('/byoa/mcp/')) return agents.proxy(req)  // the MCP proxy: no app session check here
if (url.pathname === '/byoa/callback') {                               // the MCP server's sign-in page sends the browser here
  const p = url.searchParams
  await agents.finishMcp({ state: p.get('state') ?? '', code: p.get('code') ?? undefined, error: p.get('error') ?? undefined })
  return Response.redirect(`${publicUrl}/`, 302)
}
```

- The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put your app's session check in front of it: the harness in the sandbox has no app session.
- Every other route reads the user from your app's own session. The `userId` you give byoa is your app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls.

## Sign the user in to their plan

The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives your app only that page's URL and, for Codex, a code. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md) for each step.

```ts
const claude = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'claude')  // { url }: Anthropic's own sign-in page
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'claude', { code })        // the code that page shows
const codex = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'codex')    // { url, code }: OpenAI's page and the code to enter
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'codex', { waitMs: 60_000 })  // call again while the state is 'pending'
```

## Connect an MCP tool, one time

```ts
const mcp = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
// mcp.signInUrl: the server's sign-in page; your redirectUrl route then calls agents.finishMcp({ state, code })
```

Every later job of this user can have this server. Your app's own data needs no MCP server: give its tools to `createAgents` as functions. See [MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md).

## Run a job

```ts
for await (const event of agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['notion'], setup: { agentsMd, skills } })) {
  // start, text, tool_call, tool_result, permission, error, end: the same events for Claude Code and Codex
}
```

`run` does not throw when a job fails. It gives `error` events, then always one `end` event. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md) for the events, what the agent may do, and jobs at the same time.

## Let a coding agent do it

[skills/byoa](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/skills/byoa) is a skill in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format. It teaches a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Amp and others) to add byoa to an app: the install, `createAgents` with a store and a sandbox adapter, the sign-in, the MCP connections and their routes, `agents.run` and its events, and the lab rules. To install it in your app's repository:

```sh
npx skills add madeyexz/byoa              # Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others
amp skill add madeyexz/byoa/skills/byoa   # Amp
```

For LLMs, the site also serves the docs as [llms.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms.txt) (an index) and [llms-full.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms-full.txt) (the docs, SPEC.md, the example and the skill in one file), and each docs page as Markdown (add `.md` to its address).

## Next

- Read [Concepts](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/concepts.md) to learn who holds what, and where.
- Run the [to-do example](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo): an AI-native to-do list, with tests that use the fake harness.
- Test your app with no plan and no sandbox: [Testing](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md).
- Follow the [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md). Every app on byoa must.

# Concepts

**Your app brings the product. Each user brings the agent.** You build the app and pick the sandbox. Each user brings their plan and their tools. byoa runs inside your backend and runs each job in that user's own sandbox.

## Who brings what

Diagram: You build the app and import byoa. Each user signs in with their own plan and connects their tools once. Your app code calls agents.run. byoa is a library inside your app&#x27;s backend, and keeps AI logins and MCP grants in your database. Below your backend&#x27;s edge, byoa drives three things that run outside it: a new sandbox for each job at E2B or Daytona on your account, where the user&#x27;s own Claude Code or Codex runs; the AI labs, whose model calls the user&#x27;s own plan pays; and the user&#x27;s MCP servers, which get the real token from byoa&#x27;s proxy.

```text
DEVELOPER · YOU                                           END USER
┌────────────────────────────────────┐                    ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│ builds the app                     │                    │ uses the app                       │
│ picks the sandbox provider         │                    │ has a Claude or ChatGPT plan       │
│ owns the database                  │                    │ has MCP tools and skills           │
└──────────────────┬─────────────────┘                    └──────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                   │ imports byoa             signs in on the lab&#x27;s own page │
                   │                             connects each MCP tool once │
                   ▼                                                         ▼
┌─ YOUR APP&#x27;S BACKEND · you run it ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  your app code                                            your database                      │
│        │ agents.run(userId, task)                               ▲ AI logins, MCP grants      │
│        ▼                                                        │                            │
│ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ │
│ ┃ byoa · open source, Apache 2.0                                                           ┃ │
│ ┃   AI login · harness            skills · AGENTS.md            MCP OAuth · proxy          ┃ │
│ ┃              │                                                           │               ┃ │
└─╂┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄ ▲ your backend · outside it ▼ ┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄╂─┘
  ┃              │ create · run · destroy                         real token │               ┃
  ┃              ▼                                                           ▼               ┃
  ┃ ┌─ SANDBOX ────────────────┐  ┌─ AI LABS ────────────────┐  ┌─ MCP SERVERS ────────────┐ ┃
  ┃ │ E2B or Daytona,          │  │ Anthropic · OpenAI       │  │ Notion · Gmail · …       │ ┃
  ┃ │ on your account          ├─▶│ model calls, paid by     │  │ the user&#x27;s own accounts  │ ┃
  ┃ │ runs the user&#x27;s own      │  │ the user&#x27;s own plan      │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ │ Claude Code or Codex     │  │                          │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘ ┃
  ┃                                                                                          ┃
  ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
```

- **You, the developer**, build the app, pick the sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona or Instabox, on your own account) and own the database. You import byoa into your app's backend.
- **The end user** uses your app. They have a Claude or ChatGPT plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion or Gmail. They sign in on the lab's own page one time, and connect each MCP tool one time.
- **byoa** is a library in your backend. It keeps the user's AI login and MCP grants in your database, encrypted with your key. For each job, it gets a sandbox at your provider and runs the user's own, unmodified Claude Code or Codex there.
- **The AI labs** (Anthropic, OpenAI) get the model calls. The user's own plan pays for them, not your API bill.
- **The MCP servers** get the real token from byoa's proxy in your backend, never from the sandbox.

## The problem

To make an app AI-native, you run a big lab's harness (Claude Code or Codex) in a sandbox, with the user's own AI plan. For each app, you must build the same connection layer again:

- the user's AI login, through the real CLI;
- the user's MCP connections and their OAuth tokens, with one refresh owner;
- the user's skills and AGENTS.md;
- the harness install and its updates;
- the code that connects all of this to one sandbox provider.

byoa is that layer, as a library, so you do not build it again for each app.

## What byoa is, and what it is not

- byoa **is** a library. It runs inside your app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex). Cloudflare Workers support is planned.
- byoa **stores tokens in your own database**, through a store adapter.
- byoa **is not** a hosted service. We do not run a server, and we never see your users' tokens.

| | Version 1 | Later |
|---|---|---|
| Agents | Claude Code, Codex | Gemini or Antigravity, maybe |
| User plans | Claude, ChatGPT | |
| Sandboxes | E2B, Daytona, Instabox | other providers |
| Backends | Node, Convex actions | Cloudflare Workers |
| Token stores | Convex, Postgres, or your own with get, put, delete and compare-and-set | |

## How a job runs

Your app calls `agents.run(userId, task)`. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, and runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan. The [sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md) has every step and every decision.

Diagram: One job, from agents.run to the end event

1. Your app calls agents.run. `agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp, setup })`.
2. Take the user's sandbox. By default, resume the user's kept sandbox, or create it for the first job. With `sandboxPer 'job'`, create a new one.
3. Load the setup. The pinned harness, the skills, AGENTS.md, and an MCP config that points to your proxy with a job token.
4. Copy the AI login in. From your database, decrypted in your backend. Login files: login files in.
5. Run the harness. Text, tool calls and permission requests stream back as events. MCP calls go through the proxy.
6. close() This is the end. End the job token, save the login back if the CLI changed it, remove it from the sandbox, then pause or destroy the sandbox. Login files: files removed.

The user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database between jobs. A kept sandbox keeps the files that the app wrote there and the installed harness, but no login.

## Real tokens never go into the sandbox

The agent in the sandbox gets a short-lived job token, for one job and one user. The proxy in your backend adds the real MCP token to each request.

Diagram: How an MCP call from the sandbox gets the real token

1. The harness calls an MCP tool. Its MCP config points to your proxy, at `<proxyUrl>/<name>`, with the job token. It has no real MCP token.
2. Question: Is the job token good for this server? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or the job did not get this server.
3. Add the real token. From your database, encrypted with your key. byoa refreshes it when it is due, with one refresh owner.
4. Send the request on to the MCP server. This is the end. The answer goes back to the harness. The real token does not.

[MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md) has the details, and [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md) says where the user's AI login is at each step.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions

# Supported AI subscriptions

Your users bring a Claude plan or a ChatGPT plan. byoa signs each user in with the lab's own CLI, on the lab's own page, and then runs that CLI for them: Claude Code for a Claude plan, Codex for a ChatGPT plan. So a plan works with byoa when its lab lets it sign in to that CLI.

| Agent | Lab | Plans that work | Can the user's account get banned? |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Claude Code](#claude-plans-through-claude-code) | Anthropic | Claude Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise | [Read the FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#can-my-users-ai-account-get-banned) |
| [Codex](#chatgpt-plans-through-codex) | OpenAI | ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu | [Read the FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#can-my-users-ai-account-get-banned) |

Prices and plan names are from the labs' pages on 25 November 2026, in US dollars a month, before tax. The labs change them often: check [Claude's plans](https://claude.com/pricing) and [Codex's pricing](https://chatgpt.com/codex/pricing).

## Claude plans, through Claude Code

| Plan | Price | Works with byoa | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | no | The Free plan does not include Claude Code. |
| Pro | $20 | yes | A five-hour limit and a weekly limit. |
| Max | $100 | yes | 5 times Pro's usage. |
| Ultra | $200 | yes | 10 times Pro's weekly usage. This was Max 20x. |
| Team | $25 a seat (Standard), $125 a seat (Premium) | yes | Every Team seat includes Claude Code. |
| Enterprise | $20 a seat, and usage at API rates | yes | The organization pays for the usage. |

Sources: [Use Claude Code with your Pro or Max plan](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11145838), [What is the Team plan?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9266767), [Claude Code legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance).

## ChatGPT plans, through Codex

| Plan | Price | Works with byoa | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | no | Codex only in the ChatGPT desktop app, not in the Codex CLI that byoa runs. |
| Go | $8 | no | The same as Free. |
| Plus | $20 | yes | Codex in the CLI, with a five-hour limit and weekly limits. |
| Pro | $100, $200 or $500 | yes | More usage than Plus. |
| Business | $25 a seat (Standard), $125 a seat (Premium) | yes | A workspace admin can restrict how members sign in to Codex. |
| Enterprise and Edu | from OpenAI's sales team | yes | The same; the admin may also have to turn the models on. |

Sources: [Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11369540), [Codex pricing](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing), [Codex authentication](https://developers.openai.com/codex/auth).

## What every plan has in common

- **The user's plan limits apply.** A job uses the same allowance as the user's own chats and coding: the five-hour and weekly limits are shared. When the user is at a limit, the CLI refuses, and the job ends with an `error` event.
- **One plan for each harness.** A user can sign in to both, and each job names its harness: `harness: 'claude'` or `harness: 'codex'`.
- **The login belongs to your app.** A login that a user made in your app is only for your app. Another app on byoa needs its own sign-in. See [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md).
- **The labs' terms apply.** The labs restrict where an app may store the login, and OpenAI asks paid or hosted apps to apply to be partners. Read [the FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#can-my-users-ai-account-get-banned) before you launch.

## What byoa does not support

- **API keys.** byoa signs in only with a plan. An app that wants to pay for the AI with its own API key does not need byoa for the login.
- **Other labs' plans,** such as Gemini or Kimi memberships. byoa runs only Claude Code and Codex in version 1. Gemini or Antigravity may come later.
- **Sharing one login between apps.** The labs do not allow it, and byoa keeps each app's logins apart (`app` in `createAgents`).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq

# FAQ

## Can my user's AI account get banned?

It can. byoa cannot promise that it will not, because the labs decide, and their terms allow parts of what byoa does but not all of it. byoa is built to stay inside the parts that the labs allow:

- **It runs the labs' own CLIs, unmodified.** The agent is the real Claude Code or Codex, installed from the labs' own npm packages, and a test checks the binaries against those packages (V11). byoa never pretends to be another client, and never calls the labs' APIs with the user's tokens.
- **The user signs in on the lab's own page,** with the CLI's own sign-in. byoa never sees a password.
- **Each user uses their own plan, for their own work,** and one app's login is only for that app.

Anthropic's [Claude Code legal and compliance page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) allows "an end user signing in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own Claude subscription, including where a platform hosts Claude Code". But the same page also says:

- developers "may not collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens". byoa's default login stores the CLI's login files, encrypted, in your app's database ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md)).
- "Advertised usage limits for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code". An app that runs many jobs for one user can go beyond that.
- Anthropic "reserves the right to take measures to enforce these restrictions and may do so without prior notice."

OpenAI's [Sign in with ChatGPT Terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/) say that stored tokens "must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that paid or remotely hosted apps must [apply to be partners](https://openai.com/form/sign-in-with-chatgpt-interest/).

So, before you launch:

- Read the [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md), and decide where the logins stay: the default stored login, or `cliLogin` in a volume of each user.
- Apply to OpenAI's partner program if your app is paid or hosted, and ask Anthropic for an agreement if you store Claude logins.
- Keep each user's jobs to the user's own requests, at a pace that a person would use.
- Tell your users that the jobs use their own plan and its limits.

## What does an AI job cost with byoa, and with an API key?

With byoa, the user's plan pays for the model, and your app pays for the sandbox. With an API key, your app pays for every token. The model is by far the larger cost, so for an agent that runs small tasks, byoa costs your app about 18 to 300 times less.

### One small task

Take a small task in an AI-native app, such as "add these three to-dos and sort them by date". The agent makes about 20 model calls. Each call sends the conversation so far, so the inputs add up to about 500,000 tokens, of which about 90% are cache hits. The agent writes about 10,000 tokens, with its reasoning. The job takes about 5 minutes of sandbox time, from start to `close()`.

These are estimates. To get your own numbers, read the `usage` of each job's `end` event (`input`, `output`, `cached`, and `costUsd` when the CLI reports it).

**The model, at API prices** (per million tokens, from the labs' price pages on 25 November 2026):

| Model | 50,000 uncached input | 450,000 cached input | 10,000 output | One task |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-6.2 Sol ($2.00 in, $0.10 cached, $10.00 out) | $0.100 | $0.045 | $0.100 | **$0.245** |
| Kimi K3 ($3.00 in, $0.30 cached, $15.00 out) | $0.150 | $0.135 | $0.150 | **$0.435** |

**The sandbox,** 2 vCPU and 4 GiB of memory, for 5 minutes (prices per hour, billed by the second, only while it runs):

| Provider | 2 vCPU | 4 GiB | One hour | One task (5 minutes) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E2B ($0.0504 a vCPU, $0.0162 a GiB) | $0.1008 | $0.0648 | $0.1656 | **$0.0138** |
| Daytona (the same rates) | $0.1008 | $0.0648 | $0.1656 | **$0.0138** |
| Instabox ($0.004 a vCPU, $0.00225 a GiB) | $0.008 | $0.009 | $0.017 | **$0.0014** |

Sources: [OpenAI API pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), [Kimi API pricing](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/pricing/chat), [E2B pricing](https://e2b.dev/pricing), [Daytona pricing](https://www.daytona.io/pricing), [Instabox pricing](https://instabox.sh/pricing).

### For a month

A user who runs 100 such tasks a month costs your app:

| | Model at API prices | Sandbox with byoa |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-6.2 Sol | $24.50 | |
| Kimi K3 | $43.50 | |
| E2B or Daytona | | $1.38 |
| Instabox | | $0.14 |

The user already pays for their own plan, such as $20 a month for Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus, and the task uses its allowance.

### What the numbers leave out

- **Plan fees at the provider.** E2B's Pro plan is $150 a month, and Instabox's Pro plan is $20 a month with $20 of usage in it. Daytona has no plan fee.
- **A kept sandbox between jobs.** A paused or stopped sandbox costs no compute. It can cost a little for its disk: Daytona bills disk past the first 5 GiB.
- **The sign-in sandbox,** once for each user and harness, for a few minutes.
- **An agent needs a sandbox either way.** With an API key, your app also pays for the sandbox, and for the tokens on top. byoa takes the token bill off your app. An app that only chats, with no tools and no files, needs no sandbox; there an API key can cost less for small use.
- **The user's plan has limits.** A user who runs many long tasks reaches the five-hour or weekly limit of their plan, and the jobs stop until it resets.

It is also simpler: your app has no per-user token bill, no usage metering or credits to sell, and no API key for the model to keep secret.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/agent-tools

# Give your agent tools

The agent in each job is the user's own Claude Code or Codex. You decide what it can do in that job: which tools it can call, what it knows, and what it may do in its sandbox. This page shows each way, and which one to choose.

| The agent needs | Give it | Where it runs | Who connects it |
|---|---|---|---|
| your app's own data and actions (to-dos, mail, documents) | [your app's tools](#your-apps-own-tools), as functions in `createAgents({ tools })` | in your backend | nobody: the job token says which user |
| a service where the user has an account (Notion, Gmail) | [the user's MCP server](#the-users-mcp-servers), with `connectMcp` once | at the service | the user, one time |
| to know how to do a task, or your app's rules | [skills and AGENTS.md](#skills-and-agentsmd), in `setup` | files in the sandbox | nobody |
| skills and MCP servers as one package | [a plugin](#plugins) (Agent Plugins 1.0), in `plugins` | files, and the user's servers | the user, for each server |
| a shell, files, packages and the network | [the sandbox itself](#what-the-agent-can-do-in-its-sandbox), with `access: 'full'` | in the sandbox | nobody |

Name the tools of each job in its `mcp`. A job gets only the servers that you name, and none by default.

## Which one to choose

Diagram: Which way gives the agent an ability

1. Question: Is it your app's own data or action? If no: go on to step 2.
   - If yes: Your app's own tools. This is the end. `tools: { todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } }`, and `mcp: ['todos']` in the job.
2. Question: Does the user have an account at a service with an MCP server? If no: go on to step 3.
   - If yes: The user's MCP server. This is the end. `connectMcp(user, url, { name })` once, and `mcp: ['notion']` in each job.
3. Question: Is it knowledge, a how-to or a rule, not an action? If no: go on to step 4.
   - If yes: A skill or AGENTS.md. This is the end. `setup: { agentsMd, skills }`. The harness reads them from the job folder.
4. Question: Does it need a shell, files, packages or the open network? If no: go on to step 5.
   - If yes: The sandbox, with access: 'full'. This is the end. The default. The agent installs and runs what it needs in its own sandbox.
5. Write it as one of your app's tools. This is the end. An API that your backend can call becomes a function in `tools`. The agent then calls it through the proxy, and your backend keeps every key.

Keep secrets out of the sandbox. A key that a tool needs stays in your backend, in the tool's `run` or in the user's grant. Never put a token in `setup`, the task, the environment or a file: the agent can read everything in its sandbox.

## Your app's own tools

Give your app's tools to `createAgents` as functions: MCP server name → tool name → `{ description, input, run }`. A job gets a group by its name in `mcp`, as it gets a connected server. You write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  tools: {
    todos: {
      add_todo: {
        description: 'Add one to-do.',
        input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },
        run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),
      },
      list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
    },
  },
})
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

Diagram: A call to one of your app's tools

1. The agent calls todos.add_todo. The harness sends an MCP `tools/call` to `<proxyUrl>/todos`, with the job token.
2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get todos? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or its mcp did not name todos.
3. run(args, { user, job }) in your backend. `user` is the job's user, from the token. Never take the user from the arguments.
4. Question: Did run throw? If no: go on to step 5.
   - If yes: The agent gets a failed call. This is the end. With the error's message. The agent can try again or tell the user.
5. The agent gets the result. This is the end. A string as it is, and any other value as JSON.

- `input` is the JSON Schema of the arguments, which the harness shows to the model. byoa does not check the arguments against it: check them in `run`.
- Write a `description` that says when to use the tool. The model reads it to choose.
- Names: a server is lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 32; a tool is letters, digits, `_` and `-`, at most 64.
- Give a job only the groups it needs. A to-do job gets `todos`, not your billing tools.

## The user's MCP servers

The user connects a service one time, and each job that you give it can use it. The real token stays in your database, and the proxy adds it to each call. [MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md) has the sign-in routes and the details.

```ts
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // the browser comes back to your redirectUrl route
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['notion', 'todos'] })
```

Diagram: A call to the user's MCP server

1. The agent calls notion.search. To `<proxyUrl>/notion`, with the job token. The sandbox has no Notion token.
2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get notion? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end.
3. Take the user's grant. From your database, decrypted in your backend. byoa refreshes it first when it is due, with one refresh owner.
4. Send the call on to Notion's MCP server. This is the end. With the real token. The answer goes back to the agent; the token does not.

A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it. Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the sandbox that each server answers through the proxy ([When the proxy is down](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md#when-the-proxy-is-down)).

## Skills and AGENTS.md

A skill teaches the agent how to do one kind of task, in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format: a folder with a `SKILL.md` and any files it needs. AGENTS.md has the rules for every task of the job, such as your app's voice or what the agent must not do.

```ts
agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['todos'],
  setup: {
    agentsMd: 'You are the to-do assistant of Acme. Change only the to-dos that the user asks about.',
    skills: [{ name: 'weekly-review', files: { 'SKILL.md': weeklyReviewSkill } }],
  },
})
```

byoa writes them into a new job folder, where each harness reads them:

```text
~/work                          the job folder, new for each job
├── AGENTS.md                   setup.agentsMd
├── CLAUDE.md                   the same text, for Claude Code
├── .claude/skills/<name>/      the skills, for Claude Code
├── .agents/skills/<name>/      the skills, for Codex
├── .codex/config.toml          Codex's MCP config: each server at the proxy, with the job token
└── .byoa/
    ├── mcp.json                Claude Code's MCP config: the same
    └── task.md                 the task
```

## Plugins

A plugin in the Agent Plugins 1.0 format is a folder with `plugin.json`, `skills/<name>/` and `mcp.json`. Read it with `readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))` (`readPluginDir` from `@madeyexz/byoa/node`), and give it to a job in `plugins`:

```ts
import { readPlugin } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { readPluginDir } from '@madeyexz/byoa/node'

const plugin = readPlugin(readPluginDir('./plugins/research'))
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, plugins: [plugin] })
```

- The job gets the plugin's skills, and each of its MCP servers through the user's grant of the same name. So the user connects each server with `connectMcp` under that name; byoa never gives the plugin's URL to the harness, only the proxy's.
- Only Streamable HTTP servers load. A stdio server would run inside the sandbox with no proxy, so byoa skips it and lists it in `plugin.skipped`.

## What the agent can do in its sandbox

With `access: 'full'` (the default), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. So it can install a package, run a script, clone a repository or call a public API, in a sandbox that is the job's alone.

- **Files stay in a kept sandbox.** With the default `sandboxPer: 'user'`, files that the agent writes outside `~/work` are there in the user's next job. The job folder `~/work` is new each time. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, nothing stays. See [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md).
- **Results come back as events.** The agent's answer is the `end` event's `result`, and its tool calls are `tool_call` and `tool_result` events. To get a file out, give the agent a tool that saves it, such as `save_report` in your `tools`, or open the job with `agents.session` and read the file yourself with `s.sandbox.run`.
- **Limit it with `access: 'read-only'`** when the agent needs only its MCP tools, such as in a mail client. It can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, but not change a file or reach the network by itself. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#what-the-agent-may-do).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login

# AI login

A user's AI login stays encrypted in your app's database, and is in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. This page shows how byoa signs a user in to Claude Code and Codex, keeps the CLI's own login files, and uses them for each job.

| The login tokens are in | They are never in |
|---|---|
| the sign-in sandbox, until byoa destroys it | what byoa returns to your app |
| your app's database, encrypted | the job's environment variables |
| a job's sandbox, only while the job runs | a kept sandbox between jobs |
| | the state, lease and pending entries in the store |

This is for the default login, `storedLogin()`. With `cliLogin`, the tokens stay in the user's volume instead of the database. byoa never uses the tokens itself and never calls the labs' token endpoints. The unmodified CLI is the only client that sends them to the lab.

## Sign-in

Your app calls `agents.connectLogin(user, harness)`. byoa starts a new sandbox for up to 20 minutes, installs the pinned CLI and runs its own sign-in. The user signs in on the lab's page. byoa gives your app only that page's address and, for Codex, a code.

| | Claude Code | Codex |
|---|---|---|
| The CLI's sign-in | `claude auth login` | `codex login --device-auth` |
| What your app shows | a link on claude.com | a link on auth.openai.com, and a one-time code |
| What the user does | signs in; Anthropic's page shows a code | enters the code on OpenAI's page |
| How your app finishes | `finishLogin(user, 'claude', { code })` with that code; byoa types it into the CLI and waits up to 60 s | `finishLogin(user, 'codex', { waitMs })`, again until the state is no longer `pending` |
| The files the CLI writes | in `~/.claude` (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`): `.credentials.json` (the tokens) and `.claude.json` (the account: email, organization, plan) | in `~/.codex` (`CODEX_HOME`): `auth.json` (access token, refresh token, last refresh time) |

Claude Code also writes a copy of `.claude.json` in `backups/` at each start. byoa removes it and does not store it.

Diagram: The sign-in sandbox, from connectLogin to the signed-in state

1. Remove an unfinished earlier sign-in. `connectLogin(user, h)` destroys this user's earlier sign-in sandbox for the harness, if one waits. Login files: no login files.
2. Create the sign-in sandbox. storedLogin: no volume. cliLogin: the user's volume at `~/.claude` or `~/.codex`. Time limit: 20 min, then the provider deletes it.
3. Install the pinned CLI and start its sign-in. `claude auth login` or `codex login --device-auth`, in the background.
4. Question: Is the lab's page shown within 30 s? If yes: go on to step 5.
   - If no: Destroy it, and throw an error. This is the end. Also when the CLI exits at once.
5. The user signs in on the lab's page. Your app shows the link, and Codex's code. The sandbox waits.
6. Your app calls finishLogin. Claude Code: byoa types in the code from Anthropic's page. Time limit: waits: Claude 60 s, Codex 0.
7. Question: Has the CLI ended? If yes: go on to step 8.
   - If no: Answer 'pending'. The sandbox keeps running. Time limit: until 20 min. Then call again: back to step 6.
8. Question: Did the CLI write its token file? Login files: login files in. If yes: go on to step 9.
   - If no: Destroy it, and return the CLI's error. This is the end. For example, a wrong code.
9. Keep the login. storedLogin: byoa encrypts the files into `ailogin/<user>/<h>`. cliLogin: they stay in the volume.
10. Destroy the sandbox. The state is 'signed-in'. This is the end. `login/<user>/<h>`. Login files: no login files.

- If the user leaves, or your app stops calling `finishLogin`, the sandbox runs until its 20 minutes end. Then the provider deletes it, with any login files in it. This is also what happens when your backend dies.
- A new `connectLogin` for the same user and harness destroys an unfinished sign-in sooner. With the default `storedLogin()`, `signOut` does not.
- `finishLogin` after the sandbox is gone answers "the sign-in ran out; start it again".
- The state (`agents.loginState(user, h)`) is `signed-in`, `signed-out` or `expired`, with no token in it.

## Where the login stays between jobs

| | In your app's database (the default, `storedLogin()`) | In a volume of the user (`cliLogin`) |
|---|---|---|
| How it gets there | byoa reads the CLI's files from the sign-in sandbox and encrypts them together with AES-256-GCM, with your `encryptionKey` or the key you give `storedLogin`. The entry's name is part of the encryption, so the entry cannot be moved to another user. | The sign-in sandbox mounts the user's volume at `~/.claude` or `~/.codex`, and the CLI writes its files there. |
| Where it is | one entry for each user and harness, `ailogin/<user>/<harness>`, as `v1.<iv>.<ciphertext>`. It is the only copy between jobs. | the volume `byoa-<app>-<harness>-<first 24 hex of sha256(user)>`, with the files as the CLI wrote them |
| In a job | byoa copies the files in and takes them out again (below). | Every job sandbox of that user and harness mounts the same volume. byoa never reads or copies the files. The store keeps only the state. |
| Providers | all | providers with volumes: E2B (when volumes are on for your team) and Daytona, not Instabox |

To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups, see [Stores and Convex](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores.md#a-table-of-its-own-for-the-ai-logins). To use the volume, pass `login: cliLogin` (from `@madeyexz/byoa`).

The labs' published terms limit where these tokens may be stored. Each app checks them: see [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md).

## One job, step by step

This is a job with the default `storedLogin()`. First byoa checks that the store has the user's login. If it does not, the job stops with `LoginError` (in `run`, an `error` event with code `signed-out`) and the state becomes `signed-out`. `close()` runs steps 4 to 7, also when the job failed.

1. **Take the lease.** Only one sandbox may hold a user's login at a time, because both CLIs rotate their refresh tokens. byoa writes the lease `ailoginlease/<user>/<harness>` with compare-and-set. If another job holds it, this job waits up to 10 minutes (`storedLogin({ waitMs })`), then fails. The lease ends by itself after the job timeout + 5 minutes, so a lost backend does not lock it.
2. **Copy the login in.** byoa decrypts the entry in your backend and writes the files into the job's sandbox, `chmod 600`. It remembers which version of the entry it read. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `CODEX_HOME` points the CLI at them: a folder path, not a token.
3. **The CLI runs, and may refresh.** The unmodified CLI uses its tokens to reach the lab. When its access token is due, it refreshes it and writes its own files again.
4. **Save back what changed.** If the files changed, byoa encrypts them and writes them over the entry, only if the entry is still the version from step 2 (compare-and-set). If the user signed in again meanwhile, the newer entry stays.
5. **Remove the files.** byoa deletes the login files and Claude's backups from the sandbox. If it cannot delete them, it destroys the sandbox instead of keeping it.
6. **Give the lease back.** The next job of this user and harness can take it. This also happens when step 4 or 5 fails.
7. **Pause or destroy the sandbox.** With `sandboxPer: 'user'` (the default), byoa pauses the user's kept sandbox for the next job, with no login in it. With `'job'`, it destroys the sandbox.

With `cliLogin` there is no lease and no copy. The volume is mounted in the job's sandbox, the CLI refreshes the files in place, and byoa saves nothing back and removes nothing.

When your backend dies during step 3, `close()` never runs. [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#when-your-backend-dies-during-a-job) says what then stays where.

## Codex jobs at the same time: the shared login

With `login: storedLogin({ parallel: true })`, the Codex jobs of one user can run at the same time, each in its own sandbox: a `sandboxKey` for each job, or `sandboxPer: 'job'`. Claude Code jobs still run one at a time, because when Claude Code refreshes is not checked yet.

Diagram: How a Codex job takes the shared login

1. Question: Will Codex refresh the login before this job could end? Within the lease time, the job timeout + 5 min. If no: go on to step 2.
   - If yes, or not known: Hold the login alone. The job marks that it waits, so no new job joins. When the sharing jobs end, it takes the lease alone. Codex refreshes, step 4 saves the new login, and the jobs after it share again. Time limit: lease: { alone: { id, until } }, after want.
2. Share the login. This is the end. The job adds itself to the lease's shared list and gets its own copy of the login. More jobs can join. Time limit: lease: { shared: { job1: until, job2: until } }.

- To answer the question, byoa reads only the time the access token ends in `auth.json`, and no token. Codex refreshes 5 minutes before its access token ends, and that token lasts 10 days. When `auth.json` has no such time, byoa uses 8 days after the last refresh. When byoa cannot tell, the answer is yes.
- If two sharing jobs both save a change, the first save wins (step 4).
- One risk stays: Codex also refreshes when OpenAI answers 401 to a token that has not run out. If two sandboxes get that answer at the same time, both refresh, one refresh fails, and the user may have to sign in again. So sharing is your app's choice.

## Sign-out

`agents.signOut(user, harness)` deletes the user's kept sandboxes for this harness, signs out with the CLI so that the lab can revoke the login, and deletes the login.

Diagram: Sign-out, with the default storedLogin

1. Destroy the user's kept sandboxes for this harness. `signOut(user, h)` calls `deleteSandbox(user, { harness: h })`. A job in one of them ends. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Is a login stored? `ailogin/<user>/<h>`. If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Skip the CLI sign-out. Then go on to step 5.
3. Sign out with the CLI in a new sandbox. Takes the login lease alone, writes the files in, and runs `claude auth logout` or `codex logout`, so that the lab can revoke the login. If this fails, byoa goes on. Time limit: 5 min; not kept; waits for the lease, max 10 min. Login files: login files in.
4. Destroy it, give the lease back. Login files: no login files.
5. Delete the stored login. The state is 'signed-out'. This is the end. `ailogin/<user>/<h>` is deleted.

With `cliLogin`, sign-out also destroys an unfinished sign-in sandbox, signs out in a sandbox that mounts the user's volume, and deletes the volume.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle

# Sandbox lifecycle

This page shows every sandbox byoa creates, from creation to removal, with the default `storedLogin()`. A sandbox has the user's login files only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs, unless your backend dies during a job.

byoa creates three kinds of sandbox:

- a **sign-in sandbox** for each sign-in, which byoa never keeps ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-in) shows its steps);
- a **job sandbox**: by default one kept sandbox for each user, harness and `sandboxKey`, paused between jobs; or, with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, a new one for each job;
- a **sign-out sandbox**, for 5 minutes, where the CLI signs out ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-out)).

## The job sandbox

Diagram: A job sandbox, from the start of a job to its end

Kept for the user (default): `sandboxPer: 'user'`: byoa keeps one sandbox for each slot, pauses it after a job and resumes it for the next.

1. Pick the user's slot. One for each user, harness and `sandboxKey` (an empty key when none). `usersandbox/<user>/<provider>/<h>/<key>`. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Does another job run in this slot? If no: go on to step 3.
   - If yes: Wait, then try again. Time limit: max 10 min (waitMs), then an error.
3. Question: Does the slot have a sandbox? If yes: go on to step 4. If no: see "Create a new kept sandbox" below.
4. Resume it. Time limit: job + 1 min.
5. Question: Does the provider still have it? If yes: go on to step 6.
   - If no: Create a new kept sandbox. Also when it was gone (SandboxGoneError). Time limit: job + 1 min. Then go on to step 6.
6. Empty the work folder. `~/work`: nothing of an earlier job stays.
7. Question: Is the user signed in? a stored login exists. If yes: go on to step 8.
   - If no: Stop with LoginError. This is the end. The state becomes 'signed-out'. close() still runs.
8. Check the MCP servers, install the pinned harness.
9. Copy the login in. Takes the login lease, decrypts the files, writes them, chmod 600. Time limit: waits for the lease, max 10 min; lease: job + 5 min. Login files: login files in.
10. The harness runs. The CLI may refresh its login and write its files again. Login files: login files in.
   - If backend dies: Warning: If your backend dies here. close() never runs. The files stay in the kept sandbox. See below.
11. close(): save back, remove the files, give the lease back. Ends the job token. Saves the files only if they changed, with compare-and-set. Login files: files removed.
12. Question: Did byoa remove the files? any error here counts as no. If yes: go on to step 13.
   - If no: Destroy it, forget its id. This is the end. The next job of this slot creates a new one.
13. Pause it for the next job. This is the end. E2B: pause. Daytona, Instabox: stop.

New for each job: `sandboxPer: 'job'`: byoa creates a sandbox for one job and destroys it after.

1. Create a new sandbox, not kept. A new work folder. Time limit: job + 1 min. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Is the user signed in? a stored login exists. If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Stop with LoginError. This is the end. The state becomes 'signed-out'. close() still runs.
3. Check the MCP servers, install the pinned harness.
4. Copy the login in. Takes the login lease, decrypts the files, writes them, chmod 600. Time limit: waits for the lease, max 10 min; lease: job + 5 min. Login files: login files in.
5. The harness runs. The CLI may refresh its login and write its files again. Login files: login files in.
   - If backend dies: Warning: If your backend dies here. close() never runs. The provider deletes the sandbox at job + 1 min, with the files.
6. close(): save back, remove the files, give the lease back. Ends the job token. Saves the files only if they changed, with compare-and-set. Login files: files removed.
7. Destroy the sandbox. This is the end.

"Job" is `jobTimeoutMs`, 30 minutes by default. byoa gives each job sandbox job + 1 minute.

- **One kept sandbox per user (the default).** The first job of a user and harness creates it. After each job, byoa pauses it, and the next job resumes it, so files that the app wrote there and the installed harness stay. Each job gets a new job folder (`s.work`) with its own setup. One job of a slot runs at a time; another job waits for it (`waitMs`, default 10 minutes). When the provider no longer has the sandbox, the next job creates a new one.
- **Many kept sandboxes per user.** Give each job a `sandboxKey`, such as a project or a conversation. Each key has its own kept sandbox and its own lease. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#jobs-at-the-same-time) for what still runs one at a time.
- **A new sandbox for each job.** Set `sandboxPer: 'job'` in `createAgents`. Use it when nothing may stay between jobs.

In all three, the user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database. No real MCP token goes into the sandbox, a job token is refused after its job, and no copy of the AI login stays in the sandbox between jobs.

## When your backend dies during a job

- `close()` never runs, so byoa does not save the login back or remove the files.
- **Kept sandbox:** the login files stay inside until the next job of the same slot resumes it. The provider pauses or stops it later; on Instabox, it runs until 30 minutes with no activity. See the table below.
- If the CLI refreshed its login during that job, the new login is lost. The next job writes the older stored copy over the files. Because both CLIs rotate their refresh tokens, the next refresh may then fail.
- **New sandbox for each job:** the provider deletes the sandbox at job + 1 minute, with the files.
- The slot and the login lease end by themselves after job + 5 minutes, so the user's next job does not wait forever.

## How each provider pauses and times out

| | E2B | Daytona | Instabox |
|---|---|---|---|
| After a job, a kept sandbox is | paused, with no process of the job kept | stopped | stopped (not Instabox's pause) |
| A kept sandbox whose time ends (your backend died) | pauses at job + 1 min | stops after job + 1 min with no activity | has no time limit; pauses itself after 30 min with no activity (default) |
| A sandbox that is not kept (sign-in, sign-out, new for each job) | killed at its time | deleted when it stops, at the latest after its time | deleted after its time, whatever its state |
| Resume after it paused itself | byoa ends any old process first | started again; no old process runs | byoa resumes, stops and starts it, so no old process runs |
| A paused kept sandbox stays | with no time limit | until archived, after 7 days stopped | with no time limit |
| Volumes for `cliLogin` | yes, when volumes are on for your team | one shared volume, a subpath for each login | none: use `storedLogin()` |

## Removal

- `agents.signOut(user, h)` deletes the user's kept sandboxes for that harness, then signs out ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-out)).
- `agents.deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? })` on its own destroys each matching kept sandbox. A job in it ends. The login and the MCP grants stay. When you delete a user, call `agents.deleteSandbox(userId)`; when you delete a project that had a key, `agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey: projectId })`.
- Nothing else removes a paused kept sandbox.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp

# MCP tools and the proxy

The user connects each MCP tool one time, and every agent run that your app gives it has it. The real tokens stay in your database. The agent in the sandbox gets only a job token for your proxy.

## Connect a server, one time for each user

```ts
// A server with its own sign-in (MCP authorization, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE)
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // send the browser there; it comes back to /byoa/callback

// A server that takes a token the user pasted
await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.example.com/mcp', { name: 'tasks', bearer: token })

await agents.listMcp(userId)            // [{ name, url }]
await agents.removeMcp(userId, 'notion')
```

- `name`: lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 32. A job asks for servers by this name.
- The URL must be `https://` (or `http://` on localhost). With `bearer`, byoa checks the token with one MCP `initialize`, and throws if the server refuses it.
- byoa uses Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them (serve `agents.clientMetadata()` at `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`), and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not.
- The server's sign-in page sends the browser to your `oauth.redirectUrl` route, which calls `agents.finishMcp({ state, code, error })`. It finds the user from the stored `state`, so that route needs no session. A sign-in that does not finish in 15 minutes runs out; call `connectMcp` again.
- byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner: your backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time cause one refresh request. Do not refresh or read the tokens in your app's code.

## The proxy and job tokens

Serve `agents.proxy` at `proxyUrl` and at every path below it (`<proxyUrl>/<name>`). It is a fetch handler. For each job, byoa writes an MCP config in the sandbox that points to the proxy, with a job token for that one job and one user.

- The proxy checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request on to the MCP server.
- It refuses a job token after the job ends, and for a server that the job did not get.
- Do not put your app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header `x-byoa-proxy: 1`.
- No real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time. A test checks this after each job with a real MCP call ([V5](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification)).

A job gets only the servers that your app names in its `mcp`. A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it.

## When the proxy is down

Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through `agents.proxy`. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (a wrong `proxyUrl`, a tunnel that ended, a firewall), the job does not start: `run` gives an `error` event with code `mcp` and ends with `ok: false`, and `session` throws `ProxyError`. A server that does not answer gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs. Without this check, a harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.

## Your app's own tools

Give your app's own tools to `createAgents` as functions (`tools`): MCP server name → tool name → `{ description, input, run }`. `input` is the JSON Schema of the arguments. A job gets them by the server's name in `mcp`, as it gets a connected server. The harness calls them through `agents.proxy`, which checks the job token and calls `run(args, { user, job })` in your backend, for the user of that job. So you write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. What `run` returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON); when it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`: check them in `run`.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  tools: {
    todos: {
      add_todo: {
        description: 'Add one to-do.',
        input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },
        run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),
      },
      list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
    },
  },
})
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

## Move a grant into byoa

To move an MCP grant that the user already made elsewhere into byoa, call `agents.importMcp(userId, { name, url, oauth })` with the MCP SDK's state (`client`, `tokens`, `at`). Delete the old copy, so that the grant keeps one refresh owner.

## Call a service's other API with the user's grant

Some MCP servers have an API next to the MCP endpoint that is not MCP, such as an export. Your backend calls it with the user's grant through `agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'tasks', 'https://mcp.example.com/export')`: byoa adds the current token, refreshed by the one refresh owner, and gives you the response. By default, it sends the token only to the origin of that grant's MCP server. It does not follow redirects, and never gives you the token.

When the service's API is on another origin than its MCP server, name that origin in your own configuration, for the MCP server's origin. Only grants of that MCP server can go there, and only to that exact origin:

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  // Margins' MCP server is on margin.rippling.computer; its export is on its Convex site
  grantOrigins: { 'https://margin.rippling.computer': ['https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site'] },
})
const r = await agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'margins', 'https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site/ext/export')
```

The MCP server, the sandbox and the user cannot add an origin. Each one is an exact origin: https, no path, no wildcard.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents

# Running agents

Your app runs a job with `agents.run`. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan, and streams its events. For a program of your own around the harness, use `agents.session`; for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes, `agents.jobToken`.

## Run a job and stream its events

```ts
for await (const ev of agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude',                   // 'claude' | 'codex' | 'fake'
  task,                                // the user's request
  mcp: ['notion', 'todos'],            // the servers this job gets; default none
  setup: { agentsMd, skills },         // AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code); skills: [{ name, files: { 'SKILL.md': '...' } }]
})) {
  // ev.type: 'start' | 'text' | 'tool_call' | 'tool_result' | 'permission' | 'error' | 'end'
}
```

- The events are the same for Claude Code and Codex. The schema is in the [API reference](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md#events-one-schema-for-both-harnesses).
- `run` does not throw when a job fails. It gives `error` events (`code`: `signed-out`, `expired`, `harness`, `sandbox` or `mcp`), and always ends with one `end` event (`ok`, `result`, `usage`). On `signed-out` or `expired`, show the sign-in again.
- byoa writes skills where each harness reads them (`.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`), AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code) from one source, and the MCP config in each harness's own format. `plugins` adds the skills and MCP servers of an Agent Plugins package (`readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))`).
- byoa installs the pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, so a new pin reaches every user at their next job.
- If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call `return()` on the generator). byoa still ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses or destroys the sandbox.

## What the agent may do

By default (`access: 'full'`), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. This is for a sandbox that is the job's alone. An app whose agent must only use its MCP tools, such as a to-do list or a mail client, gives the job `access: 'read-only'`:

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['mail'], setup: { skills }, access: 'read-only' })
```

The agent can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, so the harness can still read its skills and AGENTS.md. It cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. byoa only sets each CLI's own options: Codex runs in its own `read-only` sandbox, and Claude Code gets only its tools that read; each tool it refuses is a `permission` event. `read-only` does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read. Use it always with `localSandbox()` on a user's own computer, where the sandbox isolates nothing.

## Sandbox modes

| | Where a job runs | Jobs of one user and harness at the same time |
|---|---|---|
| `sandboxPer: 'user'` (the default) | the user's one kept sandbox for that harness, paused between jobs | one; another job waits (`waitMs`, default 10 minutes) |
| a `sandboxKey` for each job | one kept sandbox for each key, such as a project or a conversation, each with its own lease | one for each key, but see the AI login below |
| `sandboxPer: 'job'` | a new sandbox, destroyed after the job | see the AI login below |

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, sandboxKey: projectId })  // one kept sandbox for each project
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, sandboxPer: 'job' })          // a new sandbox for each job; default 'user'
```

[Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md) shows each step of each mode, and what each provider does.

## Jobs at the same time

With the default stored login, one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time, and another job waits for it. So a user's Claude Code or Codex jobs run one after the other in every mode, also with different sandbox keys. Only the fake harness runs them at the same time.

For many Codex agents of one user at the same time, each on its own machine, with one sign-in, turn on the shared login and give each agent its own sandbox:

```ts
import { createAgents, storedLogin } from '@madeyexz/byoa'

const agents = createAgents({ ...options, login: storedLogin({ parallel: true }) })
await Promise.all(tasks.map((task, i) => drain(agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, sandboxKey: `agent-${i}` }))))
```

(`drain` is your own function that reads each job's events.) The jobs then share the login while it is not due for a refresh. One risk stays, and Claude Code jobs of one user always run one at a time: see [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#codex-jobs-at-the-same-time-the-shared-login).

## A program of your own around the harness

An app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness (for example its own server, which starts `claude` or `codex` itself) opens the job with `agents.session` instead. It gets the same sandbox, login, pinned harness and job token, and runs its own command:

```ts
const s = await agents.session(userId, { harness: 'claude', mcp: ['notion'] })
try {
  // s.bin: the pinned claude binary; s.env: its login folder, the job token and its MCP start timeout; s.mcp: [{ name, url }] at the proxy
  await s.sandbox.run(`my-server --claude ${s.bin}`, { cwd: s.work, env: s.env })
} finally { await s.close() }  // ends the job token, takes the AI login out, and pauses the user's sandbox
```

`session` throws `LoginError` when the harness is not signed in, and `ProxyError` when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy.

## A harness outside byoa's sandboxes

A program outside byoa's sandboxes, such as a harness on the user's own computer, gets a job token with no sandbox: `const t = await agents.jobToken(userId, { mcp: ['notion'] })` gives `t.token` and `t.mcp` (the proxy URLs), with the same rules as a job's token, until `t.close()`. Send `t.token` as `Authorization: Bearer` to each `t.mcp[].url`.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers

# Sandbox providers

Each sandbox provider is one adapter with one interface. Version 1 has E2B, Daytona and Instabox, and a local sandbox for development and tests. To change the provider, change the adapter that you give `createAgents`:

```ts
import { e2b } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b'
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, sandbox: e2b({ apiKey }) })   // or daytona({ apiKey }), instabox({ apiKey })
```

`e2b()`, `daytona()` and `instabox()` read their API key from `E2B_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_API_KEY` or `INSTABOX_API_KEY` when you give none. The sandbox must reach your `proxyUrl`. [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#how-each-provider-pauses-and-times-out) compares how each provider pauses and times out.

| | E2B | Daytona | Instabox | Local |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Import | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/instabox` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` |
| Package to install | `e2b` | `@daytona/sdk` | none | none |
| Between jobs, a kept sandbox is | paused | stopped | stopped | a folder |
| Volumes for `cliLogin` | yes, when volumes are on for your team | one shared volume, a subpath for each login | none: use `storedLogin()` | folders |
| Network | every public domain | Tier 1 and 2: allowed domains only | every public domain | this computer |

## E2B

Use `e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? })`. It needs the `e2b` package.

- The default template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with `404: template 'byoa' not found`. Build it one time for each pin change with `buildE2BTemplate()`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`. Any template with Node 20 or later works: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds).
- `pause` takes a snapshot of the files only where the team can (`mode: 'filesystem'`), else a full one after it ends the sandbox's processes. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit.
- A kept sandbox that times out (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not killed. When byoa resumes a sandbox that paused itself, it ends any old process first.

## Daytona

Use `daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? })`. It needs `@daytona/sdk`.

- `pause` stops the sandbox, and `resume` starts it, also from archived (more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped. A sandbox for one job is ephemeral: Daytona deletes it when it stops, and at the latest after its time.
- Daytona allows 100 volumes for each organization, so with `cliLogin` the adapter keeps every user's AI login in its own subpath of one shared volume (`byoa` by default). A sandbox mounts only that user's subpath.
- On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox can reach only [allowed domains](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits), so serve `agents.proxy` on one of them (for example `*.convex.site`), or use Tier 3 or higher. `*.workers.dev` is on Daytona's list but does not work: a Worker's address has two labels below it (`<worker>.<account>.workers.dev`), and Daytona does not resolve those.

## Instabox

Use `instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? })`. It calls Instabox's HTTP API itself, so it needs no package.

- Each sandbox starts from the `agent-browser` template (Node 22, user `user`, home `/data/home`), or from a snapshot that you name (`snapshot`).
- byoa stops the user's sandbox after each job (not Instabox's pause), so the next job starts it again with its files and no process of the last one. A sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again. A sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its `timeoutMs`.
- byoa gives a sandbox none of your account's Vault items or org Secrets, and leaves its commands out of Instabox's command history, which would otherwise keep their output (and so the AI login that byoa reads back).
- Instabox has no volumes, so `cliLogin` does not work there; the default stored login does. Instabox sandboxes reach every public domain, so a tunnel works for `proxyUrl`.
- On the free plan, a workspace has one sandbox at a time (so one user with one kept sandbox, or one job), three starts a minute (byoa waits when Instabox answers 429), and a run of 2 hours at most before Instabox pauses the sandbox.

## The local sandbox

`localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? })` is folders on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests, and with `access: 'read-only'` for a harness on a user's own computer. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux.

## Write an adapter

An adapter implements one interface ([src/sandbox/types.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/src/sandbox/types.ts)): create (with volumes), resume, run a command, write a file, pause, destroy, and delete a volume.

```ts
interface SandboxProvider {
  readonly name: string
  create(opts?: { volumes?: { name: string; path: string }[]; labels?: Record<string, string>; timeoutMs?: number; keep?: boolean }): Promise<Sandbox>
  resume(id: string, opts?: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<Sandbox>  // starts a paused one; throws SandboxGoneError when it is gone
  destroy(id: string): Promise<void>                                   // by id, running or paused
  deleteVolume(name: string): Promise<void>
}
```

- `keep: true` is a sandbox that byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider must pause it instead of deleting it, and no process of that job may run when it resumes.
- A provider with no volumes refuses `create` with volumes.
- The [API reference](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md#sandbox-adapter) has the `Sandbox` interface.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores

# Stores and Convex

byoa keeps its state in your own database, through a store adapter: MCP grants, AI logins (by default), login states, sandbox slots and leases. Grants and AI logins are encrypted with your `encryptionKey`.

## The store adapter

A store is four methods. byoa ships one for Postgres, one for Convex and one in memory for tests. For another database, write your own.

```ts
interface Entry { value: string; version: string }
interface Store {
  get(key: string): Promise<Entry | null>
  put(key: string, value: string): Promise<void>                        // writes whatever is there
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>
  cas(key: string, version: string | null, value: string): Promise<boolean>  // null: only if no entry; true if it wrote
}
```

The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant, the login lease and the sandbox slots depend on `cas`. The to-do example's `sqliteStore` in [examples/todo/todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts) is one in 19 lines.

## Postgres

```ts
import { postgresStore, POSTGRES_SCHEMA } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres'

await pool.query(POSTGRES_SCHEMA)  // once; or postgresSchema('my_table')
const store = postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) })
```

## Convex

In a Convex app, byoa's state is one table and four internal functions in your deployment (`@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex`). Call byoa from actions and HTTP actions, which can make network calls; serve `agents.proxy` from an HTTP action.

```ts
// convex/schema.ts
import { convexTable } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
export default defineSchema({ ...yourTables, byoa: convexTable() })

// convex/byoa.ts
import { convexFunctions } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions()

// in an action or HTTP action
import { convexStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa) })
```

A Convex action has a time limit, so set `waitMs` shorter than the default 10 minutes. On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, `*.convex.site` is an allowed domain for the proxy.

## A table of its own for the AI logins

To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups:

```ts
import { createAgents, storedLogin } from '@madeyexz/byoa'

// Convex: convex/schema.ts has  byoaLogin: convexTable(),  and convex/byoaLogin.ts has
//   export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions('byoaLogin')
const loginStore = convexStore(ctx, internal.byoaLogin)
// Postgres: run postgresSchema('byoa_ai_login') once
const loginStore = postgresStore({ query, table: 'byoa_ai_login' })

const agents = createAgents({ ...options, login: storedLogin({ store: loginStore, encryptionKey: loginKey }) })
```

To keep each login in a volume of that user and app instead, behind the sandbox adapter, pass `login: cliLogin` (from `@madeyexz/byoa`). Your database then never holds the login. This needs a provider with volumes; see [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#where-the-login-stays-between-jobs).

## Tests

Use `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`. See [Testing](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing

# Testing

## Test your app without a plan or a sandbox

Use `harness: 'fake'`, `localSandbox()` from `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` and `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`. The fake harness runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would, and calls MCP tools through the real proxy: each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one call. So a test proves your app's routes, grants and proxy end to end.

```ts
import { createAgents, memoryStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { localSandbox } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local'

// serve agents.proxy at http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/mcp, as in Getting started
const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp-test', sandbox: localSandbox(), store: memoryStore(), encryptionKey,
  proxyUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/mcp', oauth: { redirectUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/callback' },
  tools: { todos: todoTools },
})
for await (const ev of agents.run('u1', { harness: 'fake', task: 'call todos.add_todo {"title":"milk"}', mcp: ['todos'] })) {
  if (ev.type === 'end') assert.ok(ev.ok)
}
```

- The fake harness shows the task's first line as one `text` event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the `end` event's `result`.
- With the local sandbox, `proxyUrl` can be `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp`.
- Copy [examples/todo/todo.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todo.test.ts). Do not offer `fake` to end users in production.

## Test byoa itself

- `npm test` runs V10, V12, the fake-harness tests and the unit tests. `npm run test:v11` runs V11; it downloads about 600 MB. CI runs both on every commit.
- With `DAYTONA_API_KEY` set, `npm test` also checks the Daytona adapter against Daytona (with `BYOA_DAYTONA_VOLUMES=1` too, also its volumes; that needs a key with the volume permissions). With `E2B_API_KEY` too, it runs V4 ([test/v4.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/v4.test.ts)), which needs `cloudflared` to give the proxy a public URL. On a Daytona org on Tier 1 or 2, also set `BYOA_V4_RELAY` to a relay on an allowed domain, such as [test/relay](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/relay/convex/http.ts) deployed to a temporary Convex project.
- `npm run test:e2b` checks the E2B adapter against E2B and runs V8 there (a user's jobs in one paused and resumed sandbox, and `sandboxPer: 'job'`). It needs `E2B_API_KEY`, and with `BYOA_E2B_VOLUMES=1` also checks volumes, for an E2B team with volumes turned on.
- `npm run test:instabox` does the same on Instabox. It needs `INSTABOX_API_KEY`. `BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox` runs V4 on E2B and Instabox.

The checks V1 to V16 are in [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api

# API reference

This page is the agent skill's API reference, [skills/byoa/reference/api.md](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md), so a coding agent and you read the same text.

This is the API in https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa today (version 0.1, before version 1). It can change before version 1. The source of truth is `src/agents.ts`, `src/index.ts` and the files they import.

## Imports

| Import | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `@madeyexz/byoa` | `createAgents`, `LoginError`, `ProxyError`, `SandboxGoneError`, `memoryStore`, `storedLogin`, `cliLogin`, `harnessFiles`, `readPlugin`, `JOB_TOKEN_ENV`, `PINS`, `PACKAGES`, `ensureHarness`, `LOGIN_FILES`, `clientMetadataDocument`; types `AgentsOptions`, `RunOptions`, `RunHarness`, `ConnectResult`, `Session`, `SessionOptions`, `JobToken`, `Store`, `Entry`, `Sandbox`, `SandboxProvider`, `AgentEvent`, `Usage`, `AppTools`, `AppTool`, `Access`, `Setup`, `Skill`, `Plugin`, `LoginState`, `LoginStart`, `LoginResult` |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b` | `e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? })`, `buildE2BTemplate(name?, { apiKey?, pins? })`, `e2bTemplate(pins?)`. Needs the `e2b` package. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona` | `daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? })`. Needs `@daytona/sdk`. |
